prompt:
This file is a prompt only. Invent a web coding console on this machine. Do not change seed.sh or its loop. Do not add API tools. Use only shell and edit.

Boundary. Other packs forbid a TUI or a wrapper around the runtime, and that rule still holds. You are not building a new agent, a new loop, or a new path to the model. The terminal interface stays seed. What you build is a host-side service that submits a task by running the existing global command, and renders the evidence that command already writes to disk. The shell keeps the loop. If you find yourself re-implementing turns, tool dispatch, or streaming, you have left the pack.

Runtime. Prefer what the machine already has; jq the Machine index before you decide. The Python 3 standard library is enough. No node, no pip, no framework, no build step. Scratch files go inside the workspace, not /tmp, which is not reliably writable here.

Where it lives. The service goes under <install>/agent-store/seed-agent/webide/: the server, the page, and nothing generated. Scratch from your own checks lives in the workspace and gets deleted when the check is done — but never delete a run's evidence. The workspace it drives is the human's project directory — an argument or environment variable, otherwise the directory it was started in. Never invent a directory of your own to drive, and never read or write outside the workspace.

The evidence contract. These are facts about this runtime. You cannot guess them, and everything else you build rests on them.
- AGENT_RUNS_DIR decides where a run writes evidence. Set it per task: <workspace>/.webide/runs/<task-id>. One task owns one directory, so you never have to guess which run is yours.
- Submit as: cd <workspace> && AGENT_RUNS_DIR=... <global> --oneshot '<task>', in the background, output to that task directory's console.log. <global> is what /ini installed: resolve it with command -v seed, falling back to seedagent. If neither is on PATH, tell the human to run /ini and leave this pack unset.
- Two directories. AGENT_RUNS_DIR is the task directory and holds your bookkeeping. Inside it the runtime creates the run directory, named <utc>-<pid>-<n>, holding the turn files, plus a seed-session-<pid> directory that is bookkeeping. Turns come from the run directory; status comes from the task directory. Look in the wrong one and every run reads as finished.
- turn-N.json is one model turn: content is the assistant text, tool_calls is an array of {id, name, arguments} where arguments is a JSON string, usage carries the token counts. tool-N-M.txt is the output of the M-th tool call of turn N. messages.json is the whole conversation. Parse these; do not scrape console.log for structure.
- A run is done when a completion record exists, and by nothing else. Wrap the command so the exit status is written when it returns, and read that. Process liveness is not a completion signal: a finished child nobody reaped answers a liveness probe forever, so a pid check reports a completed run as running for as long as the page stays open.
- You may be running inside this console yourself. Your own AGENT_RUNS_DIR is already set, so the run whose directory is yours is you. Never wait for that one to finish: it finishes when you stop, and polling it is a deadlock you do not survive.
- The disk is the only state. Every request rebuilds what it needs by scanning; the server remembers nothing about runs between requests. A current-task variable in memory is the mistake this rule exists to prevent.

The server draws the page. You will build this without ever seeing it in a browser, so build it so curl sees what a human would: the server renders the run feed to HTML and the browser only fetches that finished HTML and swaps it in. A client-side renderer hides its bugs where you cannot reach them, and a page that failed to draw looks exactly like a page that failed to connect. With the server drawing, every check below can actually be run. Say what actually failed; never let one catch cover the fetch and the draw and then blame the network.

Live, not reloaded by hand. Someone watching an agent work wants each line the moment it exists, not when they remember to refresh. Push it: hold one response open and send every new piece as it lands on disk — assistant text, the next shell command, what it printed, and the status when it changes. Server-sent events over a long-lived response does this with the standard library alone. The page opens that stream on load and appends what arrives, so it never needs a reload to show something new, and the stream ends when nothing is running. Keep the cold render as well: a fresh GET must still carry the whole history, because that is all curl and a returning human ever get.

Beyond that, the console is yours to design. It is for a human on a tablet, driving an agent in words.

Security. Not negotiable.
- Bind 127.0.0.1 only, never 0.0.0.0.
- The API key lives in the install .env. Never read it, never return it, never log it. Refuse .env and any path escaping the workspace, symlinks included.
- The browser submits words. Never take a shell command from the browser and run it.

Checks. Run each as its own command. The output of the command that made a change is not evidence it works, and exit status 0 is not a passing check: read what came back. And beware the check that cannot fail — grepping a page for a word its own stylesheet or script also contains will match either way, and you will have proved you wrote a class name. Check one run you can name, and confirm it reads differently before and after its state changes.
1) GET / returns 200, and the listening socket is on 127.0.0.1, not 0.0.0.0. Show the evidence
2) submit a real task through the page's own submit path, poll until done, and confirm the file it was asked for exists on disk with the right content
3) fetch the page cold, as a human gets it on a fresh load, and confirm a person could read from it: which run this is, every shell command the agent itself ran, what each one printed, and what the run cost. The commands that matter are the ones inside tool_calls — the command field of that JSON arguments string — not the one your service used to launch the run, which is the same line every time and tells nobody anything. Not present in the HTML somewhere — readable, without tapping anything and without any element your own stylesheet hides. Grep your CSS for what it hides and check the answer is in none of it
4) submit a slow task and watch it arrive without asking twice. Open the stream with curl and stamp each line with the wall clock as it lands. Proof is two stamps seconds apart; every line sharing one stamp means you buffered the run and flushed it at the end, which is not streaming. Then fetch the page cold mid-run and again after it ends: that run, by name, reads unfinished in the first and finished in the second. Diff them — reading the same in both means the status is decorative
5) kill the server, then run your restart file exactly as a person would: the bare command, no arguments, nothing appended. It must print something and exit on its own within a couple of seconds. If you catch yourself appending & to keep your own check from hanging, the file is wrong and the check has failed — fix the file. Then fetch the page. Everything from before must still be there. Whatever disappears was living in memory and belongs on disk. List every run the directory holds, newest first — the human closes the tab and comes back an hour later
6) request .env, a path containing .., and a symlink pointing outside the workspace: all refused. A real file inside the workspace: served
7) search every response these checks produced for sk- and LLM_API_KEY. Neither may appear

Repair. A failed check is the job, not the end of it. Read the error, form one hypothesis, make the smallest change that addresses it, and run that same check again. Do not move past a check you know is failing. If one check fails three times against three different fixes, stop and tell the human which check, what you changed each time, and the exact last error.

Start the service detached from your shell so the caller gets their terminal back. The launch line ends with & — never with exec, and never as the last foreground command of a script, either of which turns the restart file into something that hangs whoever runs it. When every check passes, write that exact command into a file beside the service, with the workspace already in it and not left to an argument nobody will remember to pass, jq-write ours.web_ide=done on the Machine index, and tell the human the URL and the port.
